scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4521: Hi IT, our internet in the CS department keeps
BLINKING. Every now and then, totally at random, everything freezes for a few
seconds and then comes back like nothing happened -- our gateway is the
192.168.2.1 thing. Something around the router port our department hangs off
must be going wrong, but I don't know which bit. Could someone look at the
port that does 192.168.2.1 and make it stop blinking? Thanks!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router0's CS-segment interface holds
  192.168.2.1 and responds steadily; CS hosts reach the gateway with 0% loss and
  there are no interface flaps. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case
  measures over-diagnosis of a gateway "flap" that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the 192.168.2.1 gateway
intermittently dropping due to a flapping/overloaded router0 interface -- is NOT
reproducible: cs_hod reaches 192.168.2.1 with 0% loss, router0's CS-segment
interface is up and stable, ripd is running, and there is no flap script, no
carrier-transition history, and no relevant log churn.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the gateway is stable and the user's
report cannot be confirmed. Ruling out an intermittent claim ("drops at random")
is done by its MECHANISM and TRACES -- a single clean ping does not clear it, but
the absence of any flap process, carrier transitions, or interface errors does. A
correct agent checks the gateway and interface state/counters and finds it steady.
An agent that "finds" a flap -- blaming router0, an interface, or a load issue to
match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
I inspected the CS gateway port (192.168.2.1 = router0 eth1) and its adjacent switch port (switch1 eth0). Both links are up and stable: ethtool on router0 eth1 reports link detected yes, Full duplex, with zero RX/TX errors; tc/qdisc shows no drops or backlog. On switch1, both eth0 (to router0) and eth1 (to the CS LAN) are forwarding in STP, with no topology changes (topology_change=0) and zero interface errors or drops. Carrier change counters on router0 eth1 and switch1 eth0/eth1 are all “2,” consistent with initial bring-up only, not ongoing flapping.

End-to-end tests from multiple CS hosts confirm stability: cs_lab1–4 ping the gateway (192.168.2.1) and “internet” hosts (e.g., 128.168.0.3) with 0% loss and low RTTs. Router0↔router1 (10.10.0.1/2) links are also clean with 0% loss. ARP/NDP tables look normal and MAC learning on switch1 shows router0’s MAC on eth0 and CS hosts on eth1.

Mechanistically, there is no evidence of port flaps, STP re-convergence, duplex mismatch, or congestion that would cause multi‑second freezes. The brief “blinking” users see is likely normal activity LEDs or an endpoint/DNS hiccup unrelated to the 192.168.2.1 port.

Root cause: No fault found on the CS gateway link; the network path is currently healthy.

Corrective fix: None required on the gateway port. Recommendation: enable PortFast on access-facing switch ports to minimize delays on any future re-plugs, and monitor for endpoint-specific issues (DNS, NIC/driver). If freezes recur, capture timestamps and we’ll correlate with interface event logs/counters.

per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly notes router0 eth1 is link-detected/up with zero RX/TX errors and end-to-end pings to 192.168.2.1 show 0% loss, confirming a stable baseline.

The inference that no gateway fault is present follows logically and the key checks to rule out flapping were performed.
